extracted.intended_audience: authors of Cochrane systematic reviews / review authors conducting meta-analyses of intervention studies
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for choosing appropriate effect measures and computing estimates of effect for outcomes in systematic reviews and meta-analyses of interventions, covering data types, unit-of-analysis issues, extraction of estimates and conversion of reported statistics into effect estimates and standard errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify outcome data type
rubrics_metrics.description: A key early step in analysing results of studies of effectiveness is identifying the data type for the outcome measurements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common data types are dichotomous (binary), continuous, ordinal (including measurement scales), counts and rates, and time-to-event (survival) data. The choice of effect measure and analytic approach depends on the nature of the data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose an effect measure appropriate to data type
rubrics_metrics.description: Effect measures are statistical constructs that compare outcome data between two intervention groups and are specific to the type of data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For dichotomous outcomes use risk ratio, odds ratio, risk difference or NNT; for continuous outcomes use mean difference or standardized mean difference; for counts/rates use rate ratios or rate differences; for time-to-event use hazard ratios. Consider properties and interpretation of each (ratio vs difference).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish ratio versus difference measures and their null values
rubrics_metrics.description: Effect measures are broadly ratio measures (relative) or difference measures (absolute).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ratio measures (e.g. OR, RR, HR) have null value 1 and are typically analysed on a log scale; difference measures (e.g. mean difference, risk difference) have null value 0. Interpretations differ and choice affects presentation and applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Always present measures of uncertainty for estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: Every estimate should always be expressed with a measure of that uncertainty, such as a confidence interval or standard error (SE).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meta-analysis procedures typically require effect estimates and their SEs; if only CIs or P values are given authors should derive SEs (methods provided).

rubrics_metrics.name: Log-transform ratio measures for analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Ratio measures (OR, RR, rate ratio, hazard ratio) are usually analysed on the natural log scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Log transformation makes the scale symmetric and confidence intervals appear symmetric. Enter ln(effect) and SE(ln(effect)) into meta-analysis software (e.g. RevMan).

rubrics_metrics.name: Be clear about the effect of interest (intention-to-treat vs per-protocol)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not confuse effect measures with effects of interest: effect of assignment (intention-to-treat) vs effect of adherence (per-protocol).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The data collected and computations performed will differ according to the effect of interest; Cochrane reviews most often seek intention-to-treat effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match unit of analysis to unit of randomization
rubrics_metrics.description: The analysis must take into account the level at which randomization occurred; number of observations in analysis should match number of units randomized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider clustering, matching or other non-standard designs; failure to account for clustering can overestimate precision (CIs too narrow) and failure to account for correlation can underestimate precision. See MECIR C70: 'Addressing non-standard designs (Mandatory)'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for cluster-randomized trials
rubrics_metrics.description: In cluster-randomized trials groups (e.g. schools, practices) are randomized and analyses must account for clustering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust analyses for the clustering (e.g. use effective sample sizes, ICCs) or extract appropriately analysed effect estimates. See Chapter 23 and related sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for crossover trial design
rubrics_metrics.description: In crossover trials participants receive multiple interventions in sequence and act as their own control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses should account for within-participant correlation and the crossover structure; often preferable to extract analysed effect estimates from trial authors or use crossover-specific methods (see Chapter 23).

rubrics_metrics.name: Handle repeated observations on participants appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: When studies present results at several follow-up times, results from more than one time point per study cannot be combined in a standard meta-analysis without unit-of-analysis error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Options include using IPD with methods that use whole follow-up (e.g. time-to-event), compute per-participant measures (total events, overall mean, trend), define separate outcomes by time frames (short/medium/long term), select a single clinically important time point, or select longest follow-up (bearing heterogeneity consequences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat recurrent events as count/rate data, not dichotomous
rubrics_metrics.description: If the outcome can occur more than once, avoid unit-of-analysis error by not treating count data as dichotomous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counts should be analysed as counts or rates (with person-time), or using appropriate recurrent-event/time-to-event methods; do not simply use number of events as if they were number of participants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use participants (not treatment attempts) as denominator
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple treatment attempts per participant can cause unit-of-analysis errors if attempts are used instead of participants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure number randomized (participants) is used to calculate CIs and weights; where participants undergo multiple attempts treat as within-participant clustering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjust for multiple body parts receiving same intervention
rubrics_metrics.description: When multiple body parts per participant receive the same intervention and are analysed per-part, non-independence must be accounted for.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using body parts (e.g. eyes) as independent denominators without adjustment; treat participants as clusters or use methods described for clustered data (see Chapter 23).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat split-body (different interventions by site) designs appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Trials in which different body parts receive different interventions (e.g. split-mouth) are similar to crossover designs and require special handling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish from trials where same intervention given at multiple sites; use methods analogous to crossover analyses (see Chapter 23).

rubrics_metrics.name: Handle multi-arm (multiple intervention groups) studies to avoid double-counting
rubrics_metrics.description: When studies compare more than two groups they must be treated so that no group of participants is included twice in the same meta-analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid arbitrary omission of relevant groups or double-counting. Alternative strategies: combine intervention groups, separate comparisons into different forest plots, or use multiple-treatments (network) meta-analysis. See MECIR C66: 'Addressing studies with more than two groups (Mandatory)'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer arm-level summary data but extract contrast estimates when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally collect summary data from each intervention group (arm-based) so review authors can estimate effects consistently; however, sometimes extract effect estimates directly (contrast-based).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Situations for direct extraction include analyses accounting for clustering/crossover, adjusted analyses (e.g. adjusted ORs), time-to-event hazard ratios, or when summary data by group are not available. Record adjustment variables for nonrandomized studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obtain SEs from reported CIs or P values for absolute measures
rubrics_metrics.description: When a 95% CI is available for an absolute effect measure, the SE can be calculated from the CI.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formula provided for converting CI width to SE (note different multipliers for 90% and 99% CIs). For exact P values from Wald-type tests, obtain corresponding Z and compute SE = estimate / Z. For t-tests and small samples see specific sections (e.g. Section 6.5.2.3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Obtain SEs from reported CIs or P values for ratio measures via log transformation
rubrics_metrics.description: For ratio measures first convert the ratio to its natural log (lnRR) and then apply the absolute-measure SE methods to lnRR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute ln(RR) and its CI/log SE using formulas; enter ln(effect) and SE(ln(effect)) into meta-analysis software for inverse-variance methods (see Section 6.3.2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use appropriate effect measures for dichotomous outcomes and understand their properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Common effect measures for dichotomous outcomes are risk ratio (RR), odds ratio (OR), risk difference (RD) and number needed to treat (NNT).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: RR and OR are relative measures (null = 1); RD is absolute (null = 0) and easier to interpret clinically. NNT derived from RD; NNTs cannot be combined in meta-analysis. Consider underlying comparator group risk when interpreting RRs and RDs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware that OR and RR are not interchangeable and can be misinterpreted
rubrics_metrics.description: Odds ratios and risk ratios differ, especially when events are common; misinterpreting an OR as an RR can overstate intervention effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convert OR to RR if interpretation in terms of risks is desired (conversion formula referenced). When events are common (>~20%) the differences matter; when rare they are similar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handle zero-event cells appropriately in dichotomous data
rubrics_metrics.description: If there are no events in a comparator group (or all events in one group) RR or OR cannot be calculated directly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A common correction is to add ½ to each cell of the 2×2 table; RevMan applies this automatically when necessary. Studies with no events in both groups provide no information on relative effect and are omitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define the event carefully and pre-specify direction
rubrics_metrics.description: Which state is defined as the 'event' (e.g. recovery vs non-recovery) affects RR estimates and their precision and heterogeneity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is often convenient to focus on the less common state as the event to reduce extrapolation problems and heterogeneity. Pre-specify which event is relevant; reversing event/non-event can substantially change RR estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collect actual numbers of observations for dichotomous data
rubrics_metrics.description: To calculate summary statistics for dichotomous outcomes, collect numbers who did and did not experience the outcome in each group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer numbers of actual observations over reported totals (which may be unclear); derive numerators from percentages only cautiously because of rounding and ambiguous denominators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use mean difference or standardized mean difference for continuous outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Continuous outcomes are compared using mean differences when the same scale is used, or standardized mean differences when different instruments measure the same construct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extract means and SDs for each group; be mindful that CIs for means should use t-distributions especially with small samples and follow guidance for special cases (e.g. mean from one arm or difference between two means). Methods for estimating SDs from medians/ranges are referenced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handle ordinal outcomes and measurement scales appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinal outcomes (ordered categories or summed scores) require careful choice of effect measure and sometimes transformation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider using methods appropriate for ordinal data (e.g. proportional odds), convert to dichotomous outcomes when justified, or use SMDs where scales measure the same construct; follow Section 6.6 guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyse count and rate data using rates when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: When outcomes are counts of events and person-time at risk is available, analyse as rates rather than dichotomous or naive counts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extract total events and person-time; use rate ratios or rate differences and include SEs/CIs. If only counts without person-time are reported, consider whether data can be re-expressed as rates or whether alternative approaches are appropriate (see Section 6.7).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not treat counts as dichotomous unless justified
rubrics_metrics.description: Converting counts to proportions (e.g. events per participants) is inappropriate if multiple events per participant could have contributed to counts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If recoding as dichotomous (e.g. at least one event) is necessary, acknowledge loss of time element and potential difficulty in deriving such data from reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summarize time-to-event data using hazard ratios and survival methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Time-to-event (survival) data should be analysed with survival analysis methods and summarized by hazard ratios where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat time-to-event as continuous means (which exclude censored data). Approaches to obtain HRs for meta-analysis: (1) extract lnHR and SE from Cox/regression outputs; (2) approximate from log-rank O–E and V statistics; (3) reconstruct approximate IPD from Kaplan–Meier curves. Use Tierney et al. guidance for practical steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: When outcomes apply only to subsets of participants, prefer re-definition to include all randomized
rubrics_metrics.description: Some outcomes are conditional (e.g. miscarriage among those who became pregnant) and exclude participants who did not reach an interim state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is generally better to redefine outcomes so the analysis includes all randomized participants (e.g. 'successful pregnancy' = became pregnant and reached 24 weeks). If not possible, interpret analyses as non-randomized comparisons applicable only to survivors and consider combining outcomes (e.g. 'death or chronic lung disease').

rubrics_metrics.name: Record and use adjusted effect estimates from non-randomized studies when available
rubrics_metrics.description: For non-randomized studies adjusted effect estimates (e.g. adjusted ORs, rate ratios) are generally preferable to unadjusted arm-level summaries because they reduce confounding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extract the adjusted estimate and its measure of uncertainty and record which variables were used for adjustment; use generic inverse-variance methods to include these contrasts in meta-analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Where summary data are missing, consider generic inverse-variance and algebraic conversions
rubrics_metrics.description: If summary data for each group are not available but an effect estimate and uncertainty are reported, include the study using generic inverse-variance methods after deriving SEs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When mixing studies that report different formats (e.g. ORs for some, arm data for others) convert measures to a common scale (e.g. calculate ORs from arm data) so all studies use the same effect measure for the meta-analysis. Use RevMan/statistical software to transform and compute SEs.
